steps: An increase in temperature of 1°C is greater than an increase of 1°F.
A change of 1°C is equal to a change of 1.8°F.
The molecules of a gas are in continuous random motion.
They have different kinetic energies and therefore different speeds.
Molecules also collide with one another, continually changing their speeds.
items.finalAnswer: Gas molecules have different speeds because they have different kinetic energies and continually collide.

steps: Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the particles of a substance.
A vacuum has no particles, so it does not have a temperature in this sense.
items.finalAnswer: No; a vacuum has no particles whose average kinetic energy could define its temperature.

steps: The statement is correct because heat is energy transferred from one body to another due to a difference in temperature.
A body does not contain heat; it contains internal energy.
When a hot body transfers energy to a colder body, that transferred energy is called heat.
items.finalAnswer: A hot body contains internal energy; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.

steps: The Sun is matter because it has mass and occupies space.
It consists of hot gases, mainly hydrogen and helium.
items.finalAnswer: Yes. The Sun is matter because it has mass, occupies space and consists mainly of gases.

steps: Matter consists of tiny particles which are in continuous motion.
In a solid, particles are very close together and the forces between them are strong.
Solid particles vibrate about fixed positions; a solid has a definite shape and volume.
In a liquid, particles are close together but the forces between them are weaker than in a solid.
Liquid particles can move past one another; a liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape.
In a gas, particles are far apart and the forces between them are very weak.
Gas particles move freely and rapidly in all directions; a gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume.
items.finalAnswer: Solids have closely packed particles vibrating in fixed positions, liquids have close particles that slide past one another, and gases have far-apart particles moving freely and rapidly.

steps: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.
It is measured with a thermometer.
A mercury-in-glass thermometer consists of a glass bulb connected to a narrow glass capillary tube.
The bulb and part of the capillary contain mercury, and the other end of the tube is sealed.
The tube is marked with a temperature scale.
When the temperature changes, the mercury expands or contracts and its level moves in the capillary; the temperature is read from the scale.
items.finalAnswer: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body and is measured with a thermometer. In a mercury-in-glass thermometer, mercury in a bulb and narrow capillary expands or contracts, and its level is read against a marked scale.

steps: The three commonly used temperature scales are Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin.
On the Celsius scale, the ice point is 0°C and the steam point is 100°C; there are 100 equal divisions between them.
On the Fahrenheit scale, the ice point is 32°F and the steam point is 212°F; there are 180 equal divisions between them.
On the Kelvin scale, the ice point is 273 K and the steam point is 373 K; there are 100 equal divisions between them.
The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero; 0 K is equal to −273°C.
The relation between the scales is: C/5 = (F − 32)/9 = (K − 273)/5.
items.finalAnswer: Celsius and Kelvin have 100 divisions between the ice and steam points, while Fahrenheit has 180; their fixed points and relation are given above.
